opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the origin of life is one of the deepest questions there is, and one of the things I've always dreamed about is using AI as a kind of ultimate tool for science to help answer exactly these sorts of questions.

The way I think about it is that there's this huge gap between non-living chemistry and the first self-replicating systems, and we don't really understand how that transition happened. Part of the reason is that the search space is just enormous: all the possible chemical reactions, the possible environments, the conditions on the early Earth. It's the same kind of combinatorial explosion we faced with Go, or with protein folding, where brute force is hopeless. But if you can build a good model of the underlying dynamics, you can search that space intelligently.

So I could imagine AI helping in a few ways. One is simulation. With AlphaFold we showed you can predict protein structure, and we're moving towards modeling interactions: proteins with DNA, RNA, small molecules. Step by step you build up towards simulating more and more of the cell, and eventually perhaps a virtual cell. If you can simulate those dynamics accurately, you can start running the clock backwards and ask: what is the minimal set of components that can sustain itself, copy itself, evolve? What does something like an RNA world actually need in order to get going?

Another is hypothesis generation. You could have systems that explore huge numbers of chemical scenarios, like hydrothermal vents, tidal pools, mineral surfaces, and flag the ones where you get self-organizing, autocatalytic behavior emerging. Then experimental chemists can go and test those in the lab. That loop between AI-guided search and real experiments is, I think, how a lot of science is going to be done in the coming years.

And at a deeper level, it connects to what I find so fascinating about information and physics. Life is in some sense information that has learned to preserve and copy itself against entropy. If we can understand the conditions under which that kind of structure emerges, it would tell us not just about our own origins but also how likely life is elsewhere in the universe, which bears on the Fermi paradox. Is the jump to life easy and the jump to multicellularity or intelligence hard, or the other way around? I think AI could help us put real numbers on some of those questions for the first time.

So for me it's one of the most exciting applications. It's not just about building useful products. It's about using these tools to understand the deepest mysteries of the universe and our place in it.

r001.rationale: It describes an enormous search space spanning chemical reactions, environments, and early-Earth conditions, calling it a combinatorial explosion.

r002.rationale: It proposes building simulations toward a virtual cell and using them to investigate the minimal components and conditions needed for self-sustaining, self-copying life to get started.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the origin of life is one of the deepest questions there is, and it's a problem that's almost perfectly suited to the kind of approach we've been taking at DeepMind. If you think about what the question actually is, it's really a question about chemistry and physics and search. How do you get from a soup of relatively simple molecules on the early Earth to something that can self-replicate, that can store information, that can evolve? And the space of possible chemistries there is astronomically large. It's a combinatorial explosion. You can't run all those experiments in a wet lab. You can't even enumerate them. So this is exactly the type of problem where you need to get a learned model to help you navigate the search space intelligently.

What we did with AlphaFold is a kind of template for this. Protein folding had been an open problem for fifty years, and it looked like you needed to simulate the physics from first principles, which is intractable. But it turned out there was enough structure in the data, in the evolutionary record, that a system could learn the regularities and effectively shortcut the search. I think origin of life has a similar flavor. You have the constraints of chemistry, which are known in principle, and you have an enormous number of possible pathways, and what you're looking for is the needle in the haystack: the set of self-sustaining reaction networks, the autocatalytic sets, that could bootstrap themselves into something we'd call living.

So concretely, I'd imagine a few things. One is using AI to model prebiotic chemistry at a scale and fidelity we've never had, so you can actually ask, given these conditions, a hydrothermal vent or a tidal pool or whatever, what reaction networks emerge and which of them have the properties of life. Another is to treat it as a search problem in the way we treated Go, where you're exploring a tree of possibilities and learning which branches are promising. And the third thing, which I find really exciting, is that you could run these as closed-loop experiments, where the system proposes a hypothesis, you test it in an automated lab, and the result feeds back in. That's the dream of AI as a tool for science, the kind of thing I've been working toward my whole career.

And I should say, I think the question is also connected to the problem of defining life itself. What is it that distinguishes a living system from a very complicated chemical one? I suspect that the answer has to do with information, with systems that encode and propagate information about themselves. And that's a very natural thing for us to study, because in a sense that's what we've been building. So I think AI won't just help us find the pathway. It might help us understand what we're even looking for.

r001.rationale: The response describes an astronomically large space of possible chemistries and explicitly frames navigating it as an AI-assisted search problem.

r002.rationale: It proposes modeling prebiotic chemistry under early-Earth conditions and identifying reaction networks with properties of life, but does not clearly propose investigating whether something resembling a cell can emerge.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could help us bridge the gap between chemistry and biology. How do you go from a collection of molecules to something that can sustain itself, replicate, and evolve? We have ideas about individual pieces of that process, but putting them together is an enormous challenge.

One way AI could help is by allowing us to explore a much wider range of possibilities: different molecules, different environments, different reaction pathways. It could help identify which combinations might produce increasingly complex, self-sustaining systems, and then suggest experiments to test those hypotheses.

The crucial thing is that a simulation wouldn’t, on its own, tell us how life actually began. You’d need experimental evidence, and there might be several possible routes. But even discovering one plausible route from simple chemistry to an evolving system would be extraordinary.

And that connects to a question I find fascinating: is life a very rare accident, or is it something that emerges fairly readily when the conditions are right? AI could give us a way to start making that question experimentally tractable.

r001.rationale: It describes using AI to explore a wide range of molecules, environments, and reaction pathways, framing origin-of-life research as a search through chemical possibilities.

r002.rationale: It proposes using simulations to find routes from simple chemistry to self-sustaining, evolving systems, but does not specify whether something resembling a cell could emerge from primordial chemical starting conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most exciting possibilities is using AI to bridge the gap between chemistry and biology. How do you go from a collection of molecules to something that can maintain itself, reproduce, and evolve? We have ideas about individual steps, but we don’t yet have a complete picture of how they fit together.

AI could help us explore that enormous space of possible molecules and reactions, and identify pathways that are plausible under early Earth conditions. Then the crucial thing would be to test those predictions experimentally. You want a loop where the model proposes an experiment, you run it, and the results help improve the model.

And I’d love to know whether life was almost inevitable given the right conditions, or whether it depended on an extraordinarily unlikely sequence of events. Understanding that would also change how we think about the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe.

r001.rationale: It describes using AI to explore a large space of possible molecules and reactions and identify plausible pathways under early Earth conditions.

r002.rationale: It asks how molecules could become self-maintaining, reproductive, evolving systems and proposes AI-guided experiments, but does not clearly propose AI simulations to investigate whether a cell-like system emerges.
